overview.title: Bidirectional RNNs: the Bidirectional layer and why it fails on temperature forecasting
overview.main_topic: How a bidirectional RNN combines a chronological and an antichronological recurrent layer, how to build one in Keras with `layers.Bidirectional`, and why it underperforms a plain LSTM on the Jena temperature task but is a strong choice for text.
overview.central_idea: A bidirectional RNN runs two separate copies of a recurrent layer, one over the sequence in order and one over the reversed sequence, and merges their outputs. That gives it two different views of the data, but on the temperature task the reversed half contributes almost nothing useful while doubling capacity, so the model overfits sooner and does worse than a plain LSTM.
overview.importance: This page finishes the chapter's tour of RNN refinements (recurrent dropout, stacking, bidirectionality) with a negative result. A technique that is standard in NLP hurts here. The lesson is that an architecture's built-in assumptions, here that both reading directions are useful, have to fit the data. It also leads into chapter 14, where bidirectional LSTMs are used for text classification (p.431).
learning_objectives: Explain how a bidirectional RNN processes a sequence, using Figure 13.13: two RNNs, one on the original order and one on the reversed order, followed by a merge (add or concatenate).
Write and read Keras code that wraps a recurrent layer in `layers.Bidirectional`, and know that the wrapper creates a second, independent instance of that layer.
Explain why a bidirectional LSTM underperforms a plain LSTM on the Jena temperature-forecasting task: the antichronological half is weak and it doubles capacity.
Explain why bidirectional RNNs work well on text and other data where order matters but which direction you read in does not.
Connect the bidirectional idea to ensembling, where diverse but useful representations improve performance.
prerequisites: How RNNs and LSTMs process a sequence step by step while carrying a state (p.389-p.393)
The Jena temperature dataset, `sequence_length`, and the `train_dataset` / `val_dataset` pipeline (p.380-p.383)
The commonsense baseline and MAE as the evaluation metric (p.383-p.384)
The reversed-sequence experiment on the previous page (p.401)

summary:
The page continues the argument from p.401. An RNN trained on reversed sequences learns *different* representations from one trained on the original order, and in machine learning, representations that are "different yet useful" are worth exploiting: the more they differ, the better, because they show the data from a new angle. The authors say this is the intuition behind **ensembling**, which comes back in chapter 18.

A **bidirectional RNN** applies this idea inside a single layer. Figure 13.13 shows the input sequence `a, b, c, d, e` fed to one RNN in its original order and to a second RNN as `e, d, c, b, a`. The two RNNs' outputs are then **merged**, by adding or concatenating them. The goal is a richer representation that catches patterns the chronological RNN alone might miss.

In Keras you build one with the `Bidirectional` layer. Its first argument is a recurrent layer *instance*. `Bidirectional` creates a second, separate instance of that layer, with its own weights, and uses one copy on the chronological sequence and the other on the reversed sequence. **Listing 13.24** tries this on the temperature task. It wraps an `LSTM(16)` in `Bidirectional`, adds a `Dense(1)` regression head, compiles with Adam, MSE loss and an MAE metric, and trains for 10 epochs.

The result is negative: the bidirectional model **does worse than the plain `LSTM`**. The authors give two reasons:

1. All of its useful predictive power has to come from the chronological half. The antichronological half is known (from p.401) to perform very badly on this task, because the recent past matters much more than the distant past.
2. The extra half **doubles the network's capacity**, so the model **starts overfitting much earlier**.

The page ends by saying where bidirectional RNNs do fit: **text**, and any data where order matters but *which* order you read in does not. Around 2016, bidirectional LSTMs were state of the art on many NLP tasks, until the Transformer took over (chapter 15).

paragraphs.excerpt: the better: they offer a new angle from which to look at
paragraphs.what_it_says: This finishes a sentence that began on p.401 ("representations that are different yet useful are always worth exploiting, and the more they differ, the better"). Different representations give a new angle on the data, capture aspects that other approaches missed, and so can improve performance on a task. The authors call this the intuition behind ensembling, which they cover in chapter 18.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A model that reads the sequence backward will make *different* mistakes and notice *different* regularities from one that reads it forward. When two sources of information are both useful and not redundant, combining them gives more total information than either one alone. That is the reasoning behind bidirectional layers, and more generally behind combining several models.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It gives the principle the rest of the page depends on. It also hints at the condition that will fail on the temperature task: each view must be *useful*. Being different is not enough.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Ensembling gains come from errors that are not perfectly correlated. If two predictors have independent errors of similar size, averaging them reduces the error variance. If one predictor is much worse, combining naively can hurt. (Beyond the book.)

terminology.meaning: Combining the predictions of several different models, for example by averaging them, to get better performance than any single model. Covered in chapter 18.
The internal features or vectors a model extracts from its input. Here, the state vectors an RNN builds as it reads the sequence.

connections: p.401: the start of this sentence, and the experiment showing a reversed-order LSTM strongly underperforms even the commonsense baseline
p.396: the section preview said bidirectional layers present the same information to an RNN in different ways

paragraphs.excerpt: A bidirectional RNN exploits this idea to improve on the performance
paragraphs.what_it_says: A bidirectional RNN uses this idea to improve on chronological-order RNNs. It reads its input sequence both ways (Figure 13.13), which can give richer representations and catch patterns the chronological version alone might miss. (The last words, "cal-order version alone.", were extracted as element p402_e06 because the text wraps around the figure.)
paragraphs.what_it_means: The layer is an ensemble built into the architecture. Instead of training two separate models and averaging them afterward, one layer holds a forward reader and a backward reader, and the network learns jointly how to use both.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It defines the architecture the listing will build. The word "potentially" matters: the authors are not promising an improvement, and on this task there isn't one.
paragraphs.technical_idea: At step $t$, a forward RNN's state has seen only $x_1..x_t$. A backward RNN's state at the same position has seen $x_t..x_T$. Combining both gives each position context from both sides. When `return_sequences=False`, as in Listing 13.24, the layer returns the forward RNN's final state (after $x_T$) merged with the backward RNN's final state (after $x_1$). (Beyond the book.)

terminology.meaning: A layer made of two independent RNNs, one reading the sequence in order and one in reverse, whose outputs are merged.
Oldest timestep first, which is how all the RNNs in this chapter have processed the Jena data so far.

connections: p.401: the definition of bidirectional RNNs as two regular RNNs (GRU or LSTM), each reading in one direction, with merged representations

paragraphs.excerpt: To instantiate a bidirectional RNN in Keras, you use the Bidirectional
paragraphs.what_it_says: In Keras, use the `Bidirectional` layer. Its first argument is a recurrent layer instance. `Bidirectional` creates a second, separate instance of that layer and uses one copy for the input in chronological order and the other for the input in reversed order. The authors then invite you to try it on the temperature-forecasting task.
paragraphs.what_it_means: You write one recurrent layer, e.g. `layers.LSTM(16)`, and the wrapper makes a mirrored copy with its own weights. The two directions do *not* share parameters. Reversing the sequence and merging the outputs happen inside the wrapper, so you don't reverse the data yourself as in the p.401 experiment.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Knowing that a second, separate instance is created explains why the parameter count, and with it the capacity, doubles. The next paragraph gives that as one cause of the poor result.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Not stated on the page: Keras's `Bidirectional` has a `merge_mode` argument that defaults to `"concat"`, which matches the "Merge (add, concatenate)" box in Figure 13.13. With concatenation, an `LSTM(16)` wrapped in `Bidirectional` outputs vectors of size 32.

terminology.meaning: A wrapper layer that takes a recurrent layer instance, clones it for the reverse direction, and merges the two outputs.
A configured layer object such as `layers.LSTM(16)`, as opposed to the class `layers.LSTM` itself.

connections: p.388: the plain LSTM model this bidirectional variant is compared with
p.431: chapter 14 uses a bidirectional LSTM for text classification

paragraphs.excerpt: You’ll find that it doesn’t perform as well as the plain
paragraphs.what_it_says: The bidirectional LSTM does not perform as well as the plain `LSTM` layer. All the predictive capacity has to come from the chronological half, because the antichronological half is known to perform very badly on this task (the recent past matters much more than the distant past). The antichronological half also doubles the network's capacity, so it starts overfitting much earlier.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is a negative result with two causes. (1) The backward half reads the 120 steps from newest to oldest, so by the end of its pass the most predictive, most recent readings are the furthest back in its memory. Its output mostly adds noise. (2) The extra parameters let the model memorise the training set sooner, so validation loss reaches its minimum earlier and then rises.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shows that a stronger architecture is not automatically better. The p.401 experiment, where reversed order did worse than the baseline, was a diagnostic that predicted this outcome. The diagnostic, "is each direction useful on its own?", is worth running before adding bidirectionality anywhere.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Capacity argument, worked out (not in the book): with 14 input features, one `LSTM(16)` has $4\times(16\times(14+16)+16)=1{,}984$ weights. The bidirectional version has $3{,}968$, plus 33 for `Dense(1)` on the 32-dimensional merged vector, so about twice as many trainable parameters, while the useful signal stays the same.

terminology.meaning: Processing the newest timestep first and the oldest last.
How much a model can represent or memorise, roughly its number of trainable parameters. More capacity makes overfitting easier.

connections: p.401: a reversed-order LSTM strongly underperforms the commonsense baseline because LSTMs remember the recent past better than the distant past
p.383: the commonsense baseline (tomorrow's temperature equals today's), which is strong because recent data is so predictive

paragraphs.excerpt: However, bidirectional RNNs are a great fit for text data—or
paragraphs.what_it_says: Bidirectional RNNs are a great fit for text, or any data where order matters but *which* order you use does not. For a while in 2016, bidirectional LSTMs were considered state of the art on many NLP tasks, before the Transformer (chapter 15).
paragraphs.what_it_means: In a sentence, the meaning of a word often depends on words that come *after* it as well as before, and reading backward is not inherently worse than reading forward. Both directions give useful but different views, which is exactly the condition from the first paragraph for combining them.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It makes clear when to use the technique: for classification or tagging of whole, already-available sequences such as text. Not for forecasting, where recency dominates, and not for generation, where the future is not available (p.431).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Bidirectional models need the whole sequence before producing an output, so they are not causal. That is fine for classifying a finished sentence, but they cannot predict the next token. This is why chapter 14 notes that generation needs unidirectional models. (Inference from p.431.)

terminology.meaning: An attention-based architecture (chapter 15) that replaced RNNs as the state of the art in NLP.
Natural language processing: machine learning on text.

connections: p.431: chapter 14 builds a bidirectional LSTM for text classification and notes generation requires unidirectional models
p.474: chapter 15 discusses the Transformer, which on its own is order-blind

concepts.name: Bidirectional RNN
concepts.definition: A recurrent layer made of two independent RNNs, one processing the input in chronological order and one in reversed order, whose outputs are merged by addition or concatenation.
concepts.intuition: Two people read the same document, one from the start and one from the end, and then compare notes. Each notices things the other misses.
concepts.technical: Given $x_1,\dots,x_T$, the forward RNN produces $\overrightarrow{h}_T$ and the backward RNN, run on $x_T,\dots,x_1$, produces $\overleftarrow{h}_1$. In Keras the default output is their concatenation. The two directions have separate weights.
concepts.significance: It was standard in NLP (state of the art around 2016) and is still used for sequence classification and tagging when the whole sequence is available.
concepts.misconception: That bidirectionality always helps. On the temperature task it hurts, because the backward direction is barely useful and the doubled capacity speeds up overfitting.

concepts.name: Ensembling
concepts.definition: Combining several models (or views of the data) whose representations differ, so the combination captures aspects any single one misses.
concepts.intuition: A panel of experts with different backgrounds usually decides better than any one of them, provided each is competent.
concepts.technical: The gains come from errors that are not perfectly correlated. Covered in chapter 18.
concepts.significance: The book presents it as the motivation for bidirectional RNNs.
concepts.example: Averaging the predictions of a chronological LSTM and a model trained on different features.
concepts.misconception: That diversity alone is enough. Each member must be useful on its own, or it adds noise.

concepts.name: Overfitting (from extra capacity)
concepts.definition: When a model fits training data so closely that validation performance stops improving and gets worse.
concepts.intuition: More parameters give the model more room to memorise noise.
concepts.technical: Doubling the parameter count with an antichronological copy adds capacity without adding useful signal, so validation loss bottoms out earlier.
concepts.significance: One of the two reasons the book gives for the bidirectional LSTM losing to the plain LSTM.
concepts.example: Listing 13.24 trains for 10 epochs. The bidirectional model starts overfitting earlier than the unidirectional `LSTM(16)` of p.388.
concepts.misconception: That a bigger model is always at least as good. Without regularisation, it often is not.

concepts.name: Order sensitivity vs. direction invariance
concepts.definition: Data where order matters but the reading direction does not (text) suits bidirectional models. Data where recency dominates (weather) does not.
concepts.intuition: You can understand a sentence read backward. You can't forecast tomorrow well by focusing on last week's weather first.
concepts.technical: An LSTM's memory is biased toward the most recently processed steps. A backward reader of a timeseries therefore remembers best the oldest, least predictive readings.
concepts.significance: Lets you decide in advance whether a bidirectional layer is likely to help.
concepts.example: Text classification (p.431) versus temperature forecasting (this page).
concepts.misconception: That if order matters, both directions must be equally informative.

code.title: Training and evaluating a bidirectional LSTM
code.original_code:
inputs = keras.Input(shape=(sequence_length, raw_data.shape[-1]))
x = layers.Bidirectional(layers.LSTM(16))(inputs)
outputs = layers.Dense(1)(x)
model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs)

model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="mse", metrics=["mae"])
history = model.fit(
    train_dataset,
    epochs=10,
    validation_data=val_dataset,
)
code.what_it_does: Builds a Functional API model that reads a window of `sequence_length` timesteps of all weather features, processes it with a bidirectional `LSTM(16)`, and regresses a single temperature value. It then trains the model for 10 epochs on the chapter's training dataset, monitoring the validation set.

line_explanations.explanation: Input of shape `(sequence_length, num_features)`. In this chapter `sequence_length = 120` (120 hourly samples, i.e. 5 days at `sampling_rate = 6`), and `raw_data.shape[-1]` is the number of features per timestep (14 Jena measurements).

`layers.LSTM(16)` is the recurrent layer instance. `Bidirectional` clones it into a second LSTM with separate weights that reads the sequence in reverse. With the default concatenation, the merged output has 32 values per sample.
A single linear unit with no activation, because this is scalar regression (the temperature 24 hours later).
Wraps inputs and outputs into a `keras.Model`.
Same compile settings as the chapter's other models: Adam, mean squared error loss, and mean absolute error as the reported metric (in degrees, since targets are not normalised).
Trains for 10 epochs on `train_dataset`, evaluating on `val_dataset` after each epoch. The returned `history` holds per-epoch loss and MAE for plotting.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: batches of shape `(batch_size, 120, 14)`. Bidirectional output: `(batch_size, 32)`. Model output: `(batch_size, 1)`, the predicted temperature.
code.algorithm: Forward LSTM over $t=1..120$ plus backward LSTM over $t=120..1$, concatenate their final outputs, then a linear regression head. Trained with Adam on MSE.
code.theory_link: Puts the bidirectional idea of Figure 13.13 into code. Comparing its result with the plain LSTM (p.388) tests whether the antichronological view adds useful information here. It doesn't.

parameters.name: LSTM units = 16
parameters.role: Size of each direction's state. The merged output is 32-dimensional.

parameters.name: epochs = 10
parameters.role: Training length. The book notes this model starts overfitting earlier than the plain LSTM.

parameters.name: metrics = ["mae"]
parameters.role: Reported error in degrees Celsius, comparable with the baseline.

pitfalls: Pass a layer *instance* (`layers.LSTM(16)`), not the class.
Bidirectional layers need the full sequence, so they don't fit tasks where the model must work causally (forecasting in streaming mode, or text generation).
Capacity doubles. Consider fewer units per direction or adding dropout/recurrent_dropout if overfitting appears.
`sequence_length`, `raw_data`, `train_dataset` and `val_dataset` are defined earlier in the chapter (p.380-p.383). The listing won't run on its own.

for bidir in (False, True):

    rnn = layers.LSTM(16)

deeper.title: Why reading the weather backward is so bad for an LSTM
deeper.body:
1. The target is the temperature 24 hours after the end of the 120-step window.
2. The most predictive inputs are the *last* few timesteps; that's why "tomorrow = today" is a strong baseline (p.383).
3. A forward LSTM ends its pass on exactly those steps, so they are freshest in its state.
4. A backward LSTM ends its pass on the *oldest* step (5 days ago). The recent readings were processed first and have been partly overwritten by 119 later updates.
5. So the backward half's final state is mostly about old, weakly relevant weather. Concatenating it to the forward state adds 16 mostly unhelpful dimensions and about 2,000 more weights.

(The chain of reasoning is the book's, from p.401-p.402; the step-by-step layout is an AI explanation.)

deeper.title: Parameter count: what 'doubles the capacity' means numerically
deeper.body:
An LSTM layer has 4 gates, each with an input kernel, a recurrent kernel and a bias: $4\,(u(d+u)+u)$ parameters for $u$ units and $d$ input features.

- Plain `LSTM(16)` on 14 features: $4\,(16\cdot30+16)=1{,}984$; `Dense(1)` adds $16+1=17$, for **2,001** in total.
- `Bidirectional(LSTM(16))`: $2\times1{,}984=3{,}968$; `Dense(1)` on 32 inputs adds 33, for **4,001** in total.

That's about twice the parameters while the useful signal stays the same, which is why the model overfits sooner. (Computed here; not printed in the book.)

deeper.title: Reading a sentence both ways
deeper.body: Take the sentence "The bank was steep and muddy." Reading left to right, "bank" is ambiguous until you reach "steep and muddy". A backward reader meets "muddy" and "steep" before "bank" and resolves it immediately. For text, each direction gives information the other lacks, so combining them helps. For temperature, the 'future context' the backward reader brings is just older weather, which helps very little.

misconceptions.claim: `Bidirectional` reuses the same weights for both directions.
misconceptions.correction: The page says `Bidirectional` creates a *second, separate instance* of the recurrent layer. Each direction has its own weights, which is why capacity doubles.

misconceptions.claim: A bidirectional RNN is always at least as good as a unidirectional one.
misconceptions.correction: On the temperature task it does worse than a plain LSTM: the backward half is weak and the extra capacity causes earlier overfitting.

misconceptions.claim: Bidirectional RNNs suit any data where order matters.
misconceptions.correction: They suit data where order matters *but the reading direction doesn't*, like text. For timeseries where recency dominates, the reverse direction contributes little.

misconceptions.claim: You must reverse the dataset yourself to use a bidirectional layer.
misconceptions.correction: The wrapper reverses the sequence internally for its second instance. Manual reversal was only for the p.401 diagnostic experiment.

In Keras: `layers.Bidirectional(layers.LSTM(16))`. The wrapper creates a second, separately weighted copy of the layer.

questions.question: What does `layers.Bidirectional(layers.LSTM(16))` do with the LSTM instance it receives?
options: It runs that single LSTM twice, sharing weights, once forward and once backward
It creates a second, separate LSTM instance and runs one chronologically and the other on the reversed sequence
It doubles the number of units to 32 in a single forward LSTM
It reverses the input sequence and runs only one LSTM on it
questions.answer: It creates a second, separate LSTM instance and runs one chronologically and the other on the reversed sequence
questions.explanation: The page states that `Bidirectional` creates a second, separate instance of the recurrent layer. Weights are not shared (option 1). It is not one wider forward LSTM, although the concatenated output does have 32 values (option 3). It runs both directions, not just the reversed one (option 4).

questions.question: Give the two reasons the authors offer for why the bidirectional LSTM performs worse than the plain LSTM on temperature forecasting.
questions.answer: (1) All the predictive power has to come from the chronological half, because the antichronological half performs very badly on this task (the recent past matters more than the distant past). (2) The antichronological half doubles the network's capacity, so it starts overfitting much earlier.
questions.explanation: Both reasons are in the paragraph after Listing 13.24. The first relies on the p.401 experiment showing reversed processing underperforms the baseline.

questions.question: Why are bidirectional RNNs a good fit for text but not for the Jena timeseries?
questions.answer: In text, order matters but reading direction doesn't: backward reading gives an equally useful, different view, and words often depend on later context. In the weather series, the most recent readings are by far the most predictive, so the backward reader, whose memory favours the oldest steps, adds little useful information.
questions.explanation: The page says bidirectional RNNs fit data where order matters but which order you use doesn't. Combined with p.401's point that LSTMs remember the recent past better, this explains the difference.

questions.question: An `LSTM(u)` on `d` input features has $4(u(d+u)+u)$ parameters. With $u=16$ and $d=14$, how many parameters does `Bidirectional(LSTM(16))` have, and what is the output size with the default concatenation?
questions.answer: Each direction: $4(16\cdot30+16)=1{,}984$. Bidirectional: $3{,}968$ parameters. Output size: $16+16=32$.
questions.explanation: The two instances are separate, so their parameters add. Concatenating two 16-dimensional outputs gives 32. This quantifies the page's claim that the second half doubles capacity. (The formula is standard LSTM bookkeeping, not printed on the page.)

questions.question: Which concept do the authors name as the intuition behind combining chronological and reversed representations?
questions.explanation: The page says different-yet-useful representations offer a new angle on the data, which is the intuition behind ensembling (chapter 18). Regularization limits capacity, which is the opposite effect. Transfer learning reuses pretrained models. Data augmentation creates modified training samples. None of these is the stated motivation.

questions.question: Could you use a bidirectional LSTM to generate text one token at a time? Why or why not?
questions.answer: Not directly. The backward half needs the whole sequence, including future tokens, which don't exist yet during generation. Generation needs unidirectional (causal) models.
questions.explanation: This follows from how the layer works (it reads the full sequence in reverse) and is stated in chapter 14 (p.431). It explains why bidirectionality is used for classification rather than generation.

questions.question: Before adding a bidirectional layer to a new sequence problem, what quick experiment could tell you whether it's likely to help?
questions.answer: Train the same unidirectional model on reversed sequences, as on p.401. If reversed-order performance is close to chronological performance, both directions carry useful signal and bidirectionality may help. If it's much worse, the reverse half will mostly add capacity and overfitting.
questions.explanation: This is the diagnostic the book itself runs before Listing 13.24, and its outcome predicted the negative result on this page.
